NEUROLOGICAL__Headache:
Headache is common and usually benign, but the job is to screen out the dangerous secondary causes before pattern-matching a primary headache. Take a focused history — onset (sudden vs gradual), time course, triggers/relievers, associated features and age — and run the red flags. A thunderclap onset, fever with neck stiffness, a new headache over 50 with scalp tenderness, or a progressive headache with focal signs or papilloedema each point to a serious cause. If the red flags are clear, sort the primary type: migraine, tension-type or cluster.
🚨Thunderclap (peaks <5 min) → subarachnoid haemorrhage until proven otherwise — CT then LP (see intracranial haemorrhage). Fever + neck stiffness + photophobia → meningitis / encephalitis (see meningitis, meningism). New headache >50 with scalp tenderness / jaw claudication → giant cell arteritis — high-dose steroids now to save sight (see GCA / vasculitis). Progressive, worse on waking / lying / coughing, with vomiting, focal signs or papilloedema → raised ICP / space-occupying lesion (see raised ICP, brain tumour).

1Recognise & classify
🔍Take the history & split it
  • Onset: sudden / thunderclap (vascular) vs gradual; time course: acute, episodic, chronic or progressive
  • Associated features: aura, autonomic signs, fever, focal deficit, visual symptoms; and age (new headache >50 is a red flag)
  • First exclude a secondary (dangerous) cause, then match the primary type (migraine / tension / cluster)
🚩Red flags — secondary causes
  • Thunderclap → SAH (also CVST, dissection, pituitary apoplexy) — see intracranial haemorrhage
  • Fever + meningism → meningitis / encephalitis; >50 + scalp tenderness / jaw claudication → GCA (steroids + ESR, see jaw claudication)
  • Progressive + worse on waking / Valsalva + vomiting / focal signs / papilloedema → raised ICP / tumour / abscess (see brain tumour, brain abscess)
🟣Migraine
  • Episodic, often unilateral throbbing, 4–72 h, with nausea, photophobia / phonophobia, worse on activity
  • ± aura (visual zig-zags / scotoma, spreading over 5–60 min then resolving); identifiable triggers
  • Acute: triptan + NSAID; prophylaxis (propranolol, amitriptyline, topiramate) if frequent (see primary headaches)
🟢Tension-type & medication-overuse
  • Tension-type: bilateral, band-like, pressing, mild–moderate, no nausea, not aggravated by activity
  • Medication-overuse headache: chronic daily headache with regular analgesic / triptan overuse — treat by withdrawal
  • Reassurance, simple analgesia, address triggers / stress; limit acute medication days
🔵Cluster & other TACs / neuralgia
  • Cluster headache: severe unilateral orbital / temporal pain, 15–180 min, in bouts, often nocturnal; the patient is restless / agitated
  • Autonomic features: ipsilateral lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, ptosis / miosis (partial Horner’s); acute Rx high-flow O₂ + SC sumatriptan
  • Trigeminal neuralgia: paroxysmal electric-shock facial pain in a trigeminal division, trigger zones — carbamazepine
🩺Assess & investigate
  • Examine: BP, temperature, fundoscopy (papilloedema), neck stiffness, focal neurology, temporal arteries
  • Bloods: ESR / CRP (GCA); CT head for thunderclap / focal signs, LP after CT for SAH (xanthochromia) and meningitis
  • MRI / MR venography for CVST or posterior-fossa / progressive headache; check carbon monoxide if household / seasonal
Headache is a screening problem first: run the red flags — thunderclap (SAH), fever + meningism (meningitis), >50 + scalp tenderness (GCA), progressive + papilloedema (raised ICP / tumour). Only once these are excluded do you pattern-match the primary headache by site, duration and associated features.

Onset and company sort it: a sudden thunderclap is vascular (SAH) until proven otherwise; fever + meningism is infective; age >50 with scalp / jaw symptoms is GCA; progressive with papilloedema is raised ICP. Episodic unilateral throbbing = migraine; band-like = tension; orbital with autonomic features = cluster.

NEUROLOGICAL__Dizziness & Vertigo:
“Dizziness” is a bucket word — the first job is to classify it: vertigo (an illusion of movement / spinning → vestibular), presyncope (light-headed, about to faint → cardiovascular), disequilibrium (unsteadiness on walking → cerebellar / sensory / drugs) or psychogenic. For true vertigo, the key split is peripheral (labyrinth / vestibular nerve — usually benign) vs central (brainstem / cerebellum). The finals skill is not missing a central cause — a posterior circulation stroke — using the HINTS exam.
🚨In acute persistent vertigo, features that point to a central cause (posterior circulation stroke) are a NORMAL head impulse test, direction-changing or vertical nystagmus, a skew deviation, other brainstem / cerebellar signs (diplopia, dysarthria, ataxia, weakness) or inability to stand / walk unaided — the HINTS exam is more sensitive than early MRI (see stroke / TIA). Sudden headache / neck pain with vertigo suggests vertebral artery dissection. Do not label it “peripheral” without excluding these.

1Recognise & classify
🔍Classify the “dizziness”
  • Vertigo: illusion of movement / spinning → vestibular (then peripheral vs central)
  • Presyncope: light-headed, about to black out → cardiovascular (arrhythmia, orthostatic), anaemia, hypoglycaemia (see syncope / pre-syncope)
  • Disequilibrium: unsteadiness only on standing / walking → cerebellar, sensory ataxia, Parkinsonism, polypharmacy
🚩Central red flags (HINTS)
  • Acute persistent vertigo with a NORMAL head impulse test, direction-changing / vertical nystagmus or skew deviation → central (INFARCT) — HINTS is only valid in active vertigo with spontaneous nystagmus
  • Other brainstem / cerebellar signs (diplopia, dysarthria, ataxia, weakness) or cannot walk unaided → posterior circulation stroke (see stroke / TIA, ataxia)
  • Sudden headache / neck pain → vertebral artery dissection; consider vascular risk factors
🌀Peripheral vertigo
  • BPPV: brief (<1 min) positional vertigo on head turning / lying — Dix-Hallpike +, treat with Epley (see BPPV)
  • Vestibular neuritis: acute prolonged (days) severe vertigo, no hearing loss; labyrinthitis = the same + hearing loss / tinnitus (see vertigo & balance disorders) — but new acute hearing loss + vertigo can rarely be an AICA (labyrinthine) infarct
  • Ménière’s: episodic vertigo (20 min–hours) + fluctuating SNHL + tinnitus + aural fullness (see Ménière’s); acoustic neuroma: gradual unilateral SNHL + tinnitus
🧭Central vertigo
  • Posterior circulation stroke / TIA or cerebellar stroke — the must-not-miss cause (see stroke / TIA)
  • Vestibular migraine: vertigo with migrainous features (photophobia, headache, aura) — a common central cause
  • Multiple sclerosis (esp. young, other CNS episodes — see multiple sclerosis) and posterior-fossa tumours
💓Presyncope & disequilibrium
  • Cardiovascular: arrhythmia / heart block (see bradycardia / heart block), orthostatic hypotension (drugs, dehydration, autonomic)
  • Systemic: anaemia (see anaemia), hypoglycaemia (see hypoglycaemia)
  • Disequilibrium in the elderly is often multifactorial (vision, proprioception, cerebellar, drugs) — a falls risk (see falls assessment)
🩺Assess & investigate
  • Bedside: Dix-Hallpike (BPPV), HINTS (acute vestibular syndrome), lying-standing BP, otoscopy + Weber / Rinne, gait & full neuro exam
  • Presyncope: ECG, lying-standing BP, FBC / glucose; vertigo with central signs → MRI brain (posterior fossa)
  • Treat the cause: Epley for BPPV; short-course vestibular sedative (e.g. prochlorperazine) for acute peripheral only; betahistine for Ménière’s
Start by classifying the dizziness — vertigo vs presyncope vs disequilibrium. For vertigo, decide peripheral vs central: brief positional = BPPV; prolonged with hearing loss = labyrinthitis / Ménière’s; and any normal head impulse test, vertical / direction-changing nystagmus, skew or other neuro signs = central stroke until proven otherwise.

Timing + triggers + ears + neuro sort it: seconds & positional = BPPV; days, no hearing loss = neuritis; + hearing loss = labyrinthitis; episodic + fluctuating hearing = Ménière’s. Any central sign (HINTS / brainstem) = stroke. Light-headed near-faint = presyncope, not vertigo.

At the bedside — classify, then exclude a central cause

Decide vertigo vs presyncope vs disequilibrium; in acute persistent vertigo do HINTS — a normal head impulse, direction-changing / vertical nystagmus or skew means central
Targeted bedside tests
Dix-Hallpike for BPPV; lying-standing BP and ECG for presyncope; otoscopy + Weber / Rinne; assess gait and full neuro exam
Investigate
Central signs → MRI brain (posterior fossa / DWI). Presyncope → ECG, lying-standing BP, FBC, glucose. Audiometry for Ménière’s / acoustic neuroma

The rules that carry it: classify the dizziness first; for vertigo use timing, triggers, hearing and the HINTS exam. Peripheral = abnormal head impulse + unidirectional horizontal nystagmus + normal gait; central = normal head impulse, vertical / direction-changing nystagmus, skew or other neuro signs → image for posterior circulation stroke.

NEUROLOGICAL__Weakness:
Weakness means a genuine loss of power — first separate it from fatigue, pain-limited or apparent weakness. Then localise the lesion using tone, reflexes, wasting, fasciculations and the plantars: is it upper motor neuron (UMN), lower motor neuron (LMN), neuromuscular junction (NMJ) or muscle? Add the distribution (hemiparesis, paraparesis, quadriparesis, monoparesis, proximal vs distal). Localisation drives the differential and separates a benign myopathy from a stroke or cord compression.
🚨Acute focal weakness → stroke — FAST, urgent CT and thrombolysis / thrombectomy window (see stroke / TIA). Bilateral leg weakness with a sensory level and bladder / bowel dysfunction → cord compression / cauda equina — emergency MRI (see spinal cord compression, cauda equina). Rapidly ascending weakness with areflexia → Guillain-Barré; fatigable bulbar / respiratory weakness → myasthenic crisis — both need FVC monitoring (oxygen saturation falls late).

1Recognise & classify
🔍Confirm & localise
  • UMN: increased tone / spasticity, hyperreflexia, upgoing plantars, clonus, no wasting; pyramidal-pattern weakness
  • LMN: reduced tone, wasting, fasciculations, hyporeflexia, downgoing / absent plantars (see fasciculations)
  • NMJ: fatigable weakness, normal reflexes / sensation; Muscle: proximal symmetrical weakness, normal reflexes, no sensory loss
🚩Acute emergencies
  • Acute focal weakness → stroke (FAST, CT, thrombolysis window) (see stroke / TIA)
  • Bilateral leg weakness + sensory level + bladder / bowel → cord compression / cauda equina — emergency MRI (see cord compression, cauda equina)
  • Ascending flaccid weakness + areflexia (GBS) or fatigable bulbar / respiratory (myasthenic crisis) → monitor FVC (see Guillain-Barré, myasthenia)
🧠UMN causes
  • Brain: stroke (contralateral hemiparesis), tumour, MS demyelination (see stroke / TIA, multiple sclerosis)
  • Spinal cord: compression, transverse myelitis, MS → para- / quadriparesis with a sensory level (see spinal cord disorders)
  • Motor neurone disease: mixed UMN + LMN signs, no sensory loss (see motor neurone disease)
🔌LMN / nerve causes
  • Radiculopathy (root — myotomal weakness + dermatomal sensory loss, see radiculopathies); plexopathy
  • Peripheral neuropathy: distal symmetrical (“glove & stocking”) or a mononeuropathy (see peripheral nerve palsies)
  • Anterior horn cell: MND, (polio); facial (LMN) weakness — Bell’s palsy (see facial weakness)
🔋NMJ & muscle
  • Myasthenia gravis: fatigable weakness, ptosis, diplopia, bulbar symptoms (anti-AChR); Lambert-Eaton: improves with use, paraneoplastic (see neuromuscular junction disorders)
  • Myopathy: proximal symmetrical weakness — inflammatory (poly / dermatomyositis, see connective tissue disease), endocrine (thyroid, Cushing’s / steroids), drugs (statins)
  • Inherited dystrophies (e.g. Duchenne / Becker, see muscular dystrophies) — also proximal, high CK
🩺Assess & investigate
  • Grade power (MRC 0–5); map tone, reflexes, plantars, wasting, fasciculations, sensation and distribution
  • Imaging: CT / MRI brain (stroke / UMN), MRI spine (cord / cauda equina); NCS / EMG (LMN, NMJ, myopathy)
  • Bloods: CK (myopathy), TFTs, glucose; anti-AChR / MuSK (MG); LP for GBS (albuminocytological dissociation); FVC if neuromuscular (see MSK muscle weakness)
First confirm it is true weakness, then localise: UMN (spastic, brisk reflexes, upgoing plantars) vs LMN (wasting, fasciculations, absent reflexes) vs NMJ (fatigable) vs muscle (proximal, symmetric). Add the distribution — hemiparesis points to the brain, paraparesis to the cord, proximal-symmetric to muscle, ascending-flaccid to GBS.

At the bedside — localise, then spot the emergency
Localise the lesion
Grade power (MRC 0–5); read tone, reflexes, plantars, wasting, fasciculations, sensation and the distribution to decide UMN / LMN / NMJ / muscle
Spot the emergency
Acute focal → stroke; bilateral legs + sensory level + bladder → cord / cauda equina; ascending or fatigable + bulbar → check FVC (not sats)
Investigate by localisation
UMN → CT / MRI brain or MRI spine; LMN / NMJ / muscle → NCS / EMG, CK, TFTs, anti-AChR, LP (GBS); FVC for neuromuscular respiratory failure
